articles.title: Get it right before you send

body.support:
Nobody writes it perfectly the first time. Good writers **fix it before they send it**.

Use five steps:

1. **Plan.** Who is it for? What do you need to say?
2. **Draft.** Write it down.
3. **Revise.** Is the main point first? Is anything missing?
4. **Edit.** Use clear words. No slang.
5. **Proofread.** Check capitals, full stops and spelling.

Spell-check misses some words, like *their* and *there*.

Tip: **read it out loud**. If you get stuck, fix that bit.
body.core:
Nobody writes a perfect message first go — not teachers, not journalists, not CEOs. Good writers just **fix it before anyone sees it**.

Use five steps:

1. **Plan.** Who's it for? Why are you writing? Jot your main points.
2. **Draft.** Get it down. Don't stop to fix things yet.
3. **Revise.** Look at the big things. Is the main point first? Is anything missing? Is anything repeated?
4. **Edit.** Improve the sentences. Swap slang for clear words. Split sentences that run on and on.
5. **Proofread.** Check every word: capital letters, full stops, question marks, apostrophes and spelling.

Spell-check helps, but it misses a lot: *their/there*, *your/you're*, *off/of*. The best trick is to **read it out loud**. If you stumble, fix that bit.

Small things matter. One missing comma once helped a group of drivers win **$5 million**.

articles.vcNote: The five-step writing process and the conventions to check.

caseStudies.title: The $5 million comma

body.support:
In the United States, a law listed some jobs. These jobs didn't get extra pay for overtime. It said: “packing for shipment or distribution”.

Drivers at **Oakhurst Dairy** said: we don't pack anything, we just deliver. A comma was missing, so the law was not clear.

A court agreed. In 2018 the company agreed to pay the drivers **$5 million**.

One small comma changed the meaning.
body.core:
In Maine, in the United States, a law listed jobs that **didn't** get paid overtime. It included: “packing for shipment or distribution” of food.

Delivery drivers at **Oakhurst Dairy** said they deserved overtime. Their argument was about one missing comma. Without a comma after “shipment”, the law could mean the **packing** of food for shipment or distribution — and the drivers didn't pack anything. They only delivered.

In 2017 a court agreed the law was unclear. In 2018 the company agreed to pay the drivers **$5 million**.

One small mark of punctuation changed the meaning — and cost millions.

teacher.overview: Students learn the writing process — **plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread** — and apply the conventions of literacy (capitals, punctuation, sentence boundaries, spelling) to a real workplace text type: an email to an employer. The real case is the Oakhurst Dairy “Oxford comma” settlement.
prep: Prepare one of your own messy first drafts to model revising aloud (students love seeing a teacher's mistakes).
Optional: a real job ad from a local business for the final mission.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Nobody gets it right first go
steps: **Hook (5 min):** project the messy job email — would you hire this person?
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** the five steps; model revising and proofreading your own draft aloud.
**Read (15 min):** Get it right before you send + questions.
**Exit:** name the step for three changes.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Find and fix
steps: **Model (10 min):** fix the first two errors in the job email.
**Independent (20 min):** finish Fix the job email and Fix the sentence.
**Read aloud check (10 min):** pairs read fixes aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Polish and send
steps: **Revise, edit, proofread (20 min):** using the checklist; read aloud to a partner.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Revise, edit or proofread?** Move main point — Revise. gonna → going to — Edit. teh → the — Proofread. Missing full stop — Proofread. Add an example — Revise. Split a long sentence — Edit.

**Fix the job email:** 1 vague subject → “Kitchen hand position – [name]”; 2 too casual → “Hi [name],”; 3 → “I saw your ad for a kitchen hand.”; 4 → “I have a lot of experience. I worked at my uncle’s café.”; 5 → “Could I come in for a trial?”; 6 → add name and phone.

**Fix the sentence:** “Can you tell me what time my shift starts?” “There is a meeting on Monday at 9am.” “I worked at a café, where I made coffee, cleaned and served customers.”

**Case study:** the drivers argued the exemption only covered packing (for shipment or distribution), not distributing; the company agreed to pay $5 million (2018).
